mappings.note: Bitter as the general taste of bases is identification by an observable feature. Not LO-2, since acids are not brought in for contrast.
The soapy, slippery feel of bases is texture, an observable feature named in LO-1.
Naming red rose extract as an indicator made from petals is the coloured-flower-extract investigation LO-4 is written around.
Recall of the red rose extract colour in acid, an observation from the indicator test rather than a classification of any substance.
The basic-solution half of the same red rose extract observation.
Turmeric paper going yellow to red in a base is the turmeric test result, again an indicator observation and not LO-3, where a substance would be placed in a class.

Chuna as calcium oxide is reagent knowledge needed to prepare lime water for the activity. Kept with the other preparation items on LO-4 rather than C-SCI1.1, because the name matters here only as a step in the experiment.
Salt and water as the products is the acid plus base word equation named in LO-7 for acid-base reactions. Not LO-6, which would call for the process to be explained.
Heat as the third term completes the same word equation, so it shares LO-7 with the products item; the two together are the equation the frame names.
Naming formic acid as the ant sting acid. Competency level because no outcome covers naming the acid contained in a material; LO-13 would need the remedy, which this item does not ask for.
Moist baking soda as the household remedy for a sting is the dealing-with-acidity application. Unlike the companion item, the remedy rather than the acid is what is asked for.
Names the neutral class for substances that are neither acidic nor basic: classification by property.
Olfactory indicators as a category of test. The item is about the method, so LO-4, not LO-1, where smell would belong to the substance under test.
Explains what makes litmus an acid-base indicator, i.e. what qualifies a substance as an indicator at all.
The full chuna, settle and filter preparation of lime water is bench procedure for the activity. Not LO-13, since nothing is being applied outside the lab.

Justifies putting tap water, sugar solution and salt solution in the neutral class from the litmus evidence. Classification with a reason, so LO-3 rather than LO-4, which would cover getting the evidence.

Why an unknown must never be tasted even though acids are sour: the reason we test with an indicator instead. This is method and safety within the investigation, so LO-4 rather than LO-1, whose sour-taste feature the item is warning against relying on.
Crush, steep in hot water and filter to obtain red rose extract, the LO-4 investigation in its literal form.
How red rose extract tells acids from bases. The subject is the indicator and its two colours, so LO-4; LO-2 would apply if named substances had to be told apart.
Preparing turmeric paper from powder, paste, filter paper and drying: apparatus preparation for the investigation.
Why turmeric cannot separate an acid from a neutral solution is an evaluation of the indicator, the planning side of LO-4. Not LO-3, because no substance is being classified, only the test judged.
Explains the olfactory indicator idea through the onion strips: how the test works and what is observed.
Asks for reactants and products of neutralisation, which is the acid-base word equation. Not LO-6, since the question is framed on the equation terms rather than on the phenomenon.
Three-mark version of the ant bite remedy, still the day-to-day acidity application. Not LO-6, because relief for a sting rather than the chemistry is what earns the marks.
Why a farmer limes a field is soil treatment, named in LO-13.
Manure on over-basic soil is the same soil-treatment outcome from the basic side.
Treating effluent so it does not harm fish in a lake is minimising a pollutant, so LO-14 rather than LO-13; the beneficiary is the ecosystem.

What lichens are, a fungus and alga together, and where they grow. Identification of an organism, kept at competency level because LO-1 keys on appearance, texture and function, which this item does not use.
Listing four acidic substances from the chapter is populating a class, hence LO-3. Not LO-2, because nothing is contrasted with a second class.
The basic-substances twin of the previous item; same classification outcome.
Explains why the science-fair writing appeared, tracing the visible colour to a base meeting turmeric. Not LO-15, because the student explains someone else's trick rather than designing one.
Five-mark item covering both the conduct of the litmus activity on household solutions (LO-4) and the three-way classification the results support (LO-3). Both halves carry marks, so both are cited.

Compares litmus, red rose extract and turmeric and states turmeric's limitation; the object of comparison is the indicators themselves. Not LO-2, which would require substances rather than tests to be compared.
Explains neutralisation (LO-6) and then shows how the lemon-juice-and-lime-water activity demonstrates it in both directions (LO-4). The activity half is explicit in the question, so both are cited.

Three daily-life neutralisation scenarios with the acid and base in each: the day-to-day application outcome. LO-14 is left off because the factory case is only one of the three and the item is framed around everyday problem-solving.
First half relates hydrangea colour to soil nature (LO-5), second half asks how a gardener could change the soil to change the colour, which is treating soil (LO-13).
The curry stain turning red under soap is traced to soap being basic: an everyday phenomenon explained by its cause. Not LO-13, because no problem is solved; the stain is being read as an indicator.
Long-answer version of the turmeric-paper limitation, justified from the indicator's properties. The judgement is about the adequacy of the test, so LO-4.

Bubbles with vinegar but not soap on eggshell are related to acid reacting with calcium carbonate to release carbon dioxide. Not LO-7, since no word equation is demanded, and not LO-6, since this is not neutralisation.
Summarises P.C. Ray's contributions to science and education, the appreciate-the-scientist outcome.
Case study asking which indicator is better if an acid must also be tested, with a reason: a choice between test methods, so LO-4 rather than LO-3.
Over-liming and the corrective addition of organic matter is soil treatment in a field scenario. Not LO-6, because the remedy rather than the reaction is what is asked for.
Predicts the colour a baking-soda message will show under a turmeric spray: an expected indicator result. Not LO-15, because the design is given in the stem and only the outcome is predicted.
Neutralisation as the treatment a factory must apply before discharge, framed around protecting the fish population. Pollutant control, so LO-14 rather than LO-13.

Mixing acidic P with basic Q and naming the reaction and its products is the acid-base word equation. Not LO-3, because the classification of P, Q and R is an earlier part and this part turns on the products.
